title: Personal and family data
description: The interviewer gathers biographical data from sisters Vicki Mitchell and Bonnie Nellsch, including birth dates, addresses, and their parents' names and histories. Their mother Maxine was born in Los Angeles to fruit-following orchard workers, and their father Kenneth works as a lead burner at the smelter in Kellogg.

title: Husbands' mining work; weddings; children
description: The sisters describe their husbands, William Gene Mitchell and Lawrence, who work together as contract miners. They give their 1969 wedding dates, including Bonnie's marriage at the Hitchin' Club in Coeur d'Alene, and list their children's names, birth dates, and the hospitals in Kellogg and Silverton where they were born.

title: Education; skills; jobs
description: Both women describe their high school education, with Vicki finishing through correspondence courses. They discuss Vicki's poetry writing, Bonnie's brief 28-day stint in the Navy, and early jobs at a fabric shop, hospital, and drugstore.

title: Working after marriage; husbands' objections
description: The sisters talk about working at the hospital after their children were born and quitting because babysitting costs outweighed the pay. Both say their husbands object to them working, and one recalls her husband's reaction when she worked as a cocktail waitress, or 'tramming.'

title: First marriage and divorce; meeting husbands by letter
description: Vicki recounts her brief first marriage to Fred, her pregnancy, and the difficulty of obtaining a divorce before the baby was born. The sisters discuss do-it-yourself divorce kits and explain how each met her current husband through letter-writing while the men were stationed in Okinawa and Vietnam.

title: Crime and safety in Kellogg and San Jose
description: The women discuss whether one can walk safely at night, contrasting rough areas of Kellogg with San Jose, where car stripping was common and neighbors avoided involvement. They recall prowler and break-in incidents, police response, and the Zodiac Killer case in California.

title: Comparing family life; recreation
description: The sisters compare their current family life with childhood, noting their father's temper and new money worries. They recall camping, swimming at Rose Lake, dating, and letter-writing, and describe Bonnie's passion for bowling and the shift-work conflicts that complicate married life.

title: Hunting and fishing
description: The sisters talk about hunting and fishing in the Kellogg, Plummer, and Worley areas. They express concern about accidents and out-of-state hunters wasting game, describe a lost fish and missed grouse shots, and recall the family butchering and cooking two elk together.

title: Venison; recreation; rafting
description: The conversation begins with talk about cooking deer meat and elk in Georgia, then shifts to summer recreation. Vicki Mitchell and Bonnie Nellsch describe rafting down the North Fork river and biking.

title: Marriage expectations; children; family size
description: The sisters discuss what they expected from marriage, disillusionment with first husbands, and preferring two children. They compare their own choices with friends and cousins who had children later.

title: Birth control; marriage realism; flowers
description: They talk about sterilization, a Catholic doctor's refusal, and birth control pills. The conversation turns to how marriage differs from teenage dreams, with jokes about flowers and anniversaries.

title: Children; childcare; babysitting
description: The sisters discuss other people's children, learning childcare by babysitting, and their own pregnancies. They describe asking doctors questions and enjoying children more as they grow older.

title: Gardening; canning; bread baking
description: They recall their mother's and grandfather's gardens, canning peaches, and whether home canning saves money. They also discuss baking bread and giving loaves away.

title: Cooking from scratch; widowhood plans
description: The sisters describe cooking from scratch and avoiding canned or prepared foods. They then discuss what they would do financially and personally if a husband died, including insurance and remarriage.

title: Television; reading; military service
description: They mention watching little television and preferring Gothic novels, then recall their father's Navy service in World War II. They discuss their husbands' service in Vietnam and the lack of recognition they received.

title: Depression memories; Idaho childhood
description: The sisters recount their mother's childhood stories of living in a chicken coop near Hayden Lake during the Depression. They describe having little food, a kitten for Christmas, and smelling neighbors' bacon.

title: Depression-era childhood; grandparents' transient life
description: Vicki and Bonnie recount their mother's childhood during the Great Depression in Hayden Lake, Idaho, describing extreme poverty including lack of shoes. They explain their grandparents were transient workers who moved from orchard to orchard, making the Depression especially difficult for their family compared to established farmers.

title: Grandfather's farm life; mother's difficult childhood
description: They describe their grandfather's current retired life on a farm in Kingston and his strong work ethic, noting their grandmother recently passed away. The conversation turns to their mother's hard childhood, her hearing problem, and her bashfulness that would prevent her from being interviewed.

title: Mother's openness; father's strict temperament
description: The sisters discuss how their mother has become more open over the years, especially about topics like sex that were never mentioned in childhood. They contrast this with their father, describing him as moody and strict, recounting specific conflicts and how children had to tiptoe around him.

title: Sibling relationships; neighborhood dynamics
description: Vicki and Bonnie discuss their own relationship, admitting they fought constantly as children but are close now. They compare their neighborhoods and discuss how children often serve as the connection between neighbors, noting age differences affect community interaction.

title: Hobbies and travel; Canadian friendliness
description: The sisters list their hobbies including cooking, bowling, reading, and outdoor activities. They discuss their travel experiences, particularly praising the friendliness of people in Canada compared to more paranoid attitudes they've encountered elsewhere.

title: Outdoor interests; poetry writing
description: Bonnie describes herself as an outdoors person who enjoys fishing, hunting, camping, and rafting. She reveals she writes poetry, having written about 100 poems and attempted to get them published, including a disappointing experience with a vanity press scam.

title: Travel experiences; racial attitudes in Idaho
description: They discuss places they've traveled including Chicago and various states. The conversation shifts to racial attitudes, with the sisters noting the absence of Black residents in their area and sharing examples of local prejudice, including the Harlem Globetrotters being kicked out and discriminatory pricing in bars.

title: Husbands' mining work; Sunshine Fire
description: The sisters explain how their husbands got into mining work and discuss the constant dangers, with one husband having been in the Sunshine Fire. They describe inadequate safety improvements, health hazards including extreme heat and humidity, and the need for salt pills to prevent heat exhaustion.

title: Raising children; lead testing; views on working mothers
description: They discuss whether their community is a good place to raise children, mentioning lead testing and cleanliness precautions for their children. The sisters share their views on working mothers, with one believing mothers should stay home while acknowledging some manage both successfully.

title: Women's roles; equal rights debate
description: The sisters share complex views on women's liberation, supporting equal pay and equal opportunity but criticizing some aspects of the movement. They discuss gender roles in marriage, with one husband being controlling about appearance while another shares household duties, and debate custody issues in divorce.
